newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl nails colours to single currency mast.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl nails colours to single currency mast.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, one of Europe's fiercest champions of political and monetary integration, on Friday linked his own political future firmly to the success of the planned currency union.
"I will tie my own political fate to the founding of the European currency union," Kohl told 800 bankers at the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt.
Kohl, who last month became Germany's longest serving post-war chancellor, has long pinned his career on unifying both Germany and Europe, in the context of a currency union.
As part of that plan, Kohl said Germany, just like other nations, needed to put its own house in order, slashing deficits and tearing down antiquated labour market structures.
"The goal must be that many nations meet the stability criteria and participate in the currency union from the start.
"Today it is important to map out the path for achieving this," Kohl added, stressing the "criteria in the Maastricht Treaty must be adhered to, in the long term as well."

European countries which want to meld their currencies in the Euro from 1999 are scrambling to meet economic criteria on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt laid down in the Maastricht agreement.

Most nations are facing great problems in meeting the fiscal targets, which call for budget deficits to run at a maximum of three percent of gross domestic product and public debt at a maximum of 60 percent of GDP.
Kohl made clear in his speech that countries which want to join EMU in 1999 must demonstrate that they can meet the Maastricht criteria over the long term and without any excuses.
"The Maastricht criteria must be met without ifs and buts, and that means in the long term," he said.

Countering constant market speculation and suggestions that the Maastricht criteria could be watered down to allow more countries in, he said, "When I am talking about criteria, I mean THE criteria. Anyone who thinks that we can turn away from this chosen path is deluding himself."

Kohl has recently drawn fire from unions as he advocates putting the social welfare state on a diet as part of the training programme to pass the hurdle to enter the currency union at the end of the decade.

But he noted that Bonn's plan to narrow next year's deficit to 53.3 billion marks ($35.5 billion) will move Germany closer to meeting the Maastricht Treaty deficit criteria of around three percent of the gross domestic product.

Kohl said Europe would stick by its stated goal of basing the decision on who made the grade for EMU on the basis of actual 1997 data -- meaning that estimates, forecasts and goals would not be taken into account.
"By then everyone should have swept his own doorstep and should refrain from pointing out others' failings," he said.

Brushing aside talk that the EMU timetable exerted undue pressure on nations to whip finances into shape, putting economic growth at risk, Kohl said these efforts had to be made regardless of any ambitions to join the planned currency.
"We need to consolidate in any case, otherwise we would be paying the consequences until well into the next century," he said.
While he realised it was not easy for nations to streamline fiscal policies to meet the stringent entry requirements, he left members no choice but to push on.
"We want to do this now," Kohl said, stressing the currency union represented not only hard work but real future benefits.
